Viral
VY-rul
adjective (Millennial slang)
From Latin virus (poison, slime), viral meant "of a virus" in medicine from the 1940s. Marketing writers in the 1990s spoke of "viral marketing" (Jeffrey Rayport’s 1996 Fast Company essay "The Virus of Marketing"), and with YouTube (2005) and social media, to go viral came to mean a video, image, or post spreading rapidly from person to person across the internet. By the 2010s it was a goal pursued deliberately by marketers, influencers, and ordinary teenagers.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To go viral is to spread explosively online: a video, joke, or post shared by millions in hours, carrying its creator from obscurity to sudden fame or infamy. The metaphor is medical; the content spreads from host to host like an infection. The Christian observation: speed of spread is morally neutral, and what spreads is everything. Scripture describes its own kind of viral growth: "the word of God grew and multiplied" (Act 12:24); "the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls" (Act 2:41). The gospel has always travelled from person to person. But Scripture also knows how quickly evil spreads. "Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth" (Pro 26:20); the talebearer is the original viral sharer. Rumours, cruelty, and lies go viral as easily as truth, often more easily. And sudden fame itself is dangerous, especially for the young: the girl whose embarrassing video went viral, the boy who became a meme. The Lord Jesus often told those He healed to tell no man; He did not seek viral fame. A father teaches his children three rules: think before you share, because you are responsible for what you spread; never post what you would not want spread to millions; and if you want something of yours to go viral, let it be the good news. "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace" (Rom 10:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial-era internet sense (1990s marketing; 2005– YouTube) of content spreading rapidly person to person; morally neutral speed, so what spreads is everything: the word of God grew and multiplied (Act 12:24), and so does the talebearer’s fire (Pro 26:20).

expand to see more

VIRAL, adj. (Millennial-era internet sense, 1990s–present) Of online content, spreading rapidly and widely through sharing. To go viral. Related: viral marketing, viral video.

Webster (1828), root virus: VIRUS, noun [Latin See Virulent .] Foul or contagious matter of an ulcer, postule, etc.; poison.

Decode for parents: teach your children that every share is a choice, and that what they post can spread beyond recall.

Modern Corruption

Viral speed spreads lies and cruelty as easily as truth and hands the young sudden fame or shame; Scripture makes the sharer responsible and points to the good news worth spreading.

expand to see more

The corruption is the pursuit of spread for its own sake and the indifference to what spreads. Algorithms reward outrage, humiliation, and spectacle, and a young person can become famous for the worst moment of his life without consent. The sharer, clicking "share" without thought, becomes a talebearer at scale. The medical metaphor is apt: much that goes viral is an infection.

The recovery is responsible speech and holy ambition. Jesus told a healed leper, "See thou say nothing to any man" (Mar 1:44), because fame was not His aim. Christians should be slow to share, quick to verify, and unwilling to spread another’s shame. And they should be eager to spread what is good: the gospel, encouragement, truth. Teach the young to measure a post not by its reach but by whether it would please God if it reached everyone.
